reasons: Only 7 of 30 sections were provided for review, so most of this file was not reviewed.

terms.meaning: A check that confirms incoming data has the expected shape before the app uses it.
The rule for which industries or projects are included, such as live only or all.

sections.name: File setup, PortfolioResponse, isObj, nStr, nNum
sections.title: Imports and basic checks for the portfolio
sections.what: Brings in the data-fetching tool, the portfolio types, colors, the request helper, and the country lookup. Also defines small checks for objects, text, and numbers.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. These are the tools the validator and filters need.

sections.name: validatePortfolio, PORTFOLIO_QUERY_KEY
sections.title: Checking the portfolio response
sections.what: Confirms the server reply has the expected industries and projects, and that each one has the required fields. Any mismatch throws an error that names the bad item.
sections.why: The comment says bad data is reported, not quietly fixed.
sections.watch_out: Adding a required field on the server without updating this check will break the page.

sections.name: usePortfolio
sections.title: Portfolio fetching hook
sections.what: Provides the checked portfolio to any screen. The data is kept for one minute.
sections.why: Shares one cached copy across portfolio screens.
sections.watch_out: The one-minute freshness matches the other portfolio hooks.

sections.name: PortfolioFilters, FILTER_KEYS
sections.title: Filter settings shape
sections.what: Describes the filter settings, such as scope, industries, country, phase, company, segment, and search text, and lists the address keys used for them.
sections.why: Gives every portfolio screen the same filter names.
sections.watch_out: The address key names must stay the same as the reading code.

sections.name: readFilters
sections.title: Reading filters from the address
sections.what: Reads the filter settings from the address, using live as the default scope and treating missing values as empty.
sections.why: Keeps filters in the address so they can be shared.
sections.watch_out: Any scope value other than all is treated as live.

sections.name: scopedIndustrySlugs
sections.title: Industries in scope
sections.what: Lists the industry slugs that are visible under the current scope. If a single industry is fixed, only that one is returned.
sections.why: Lets screens show only the industries that matter.
sections.watch_out: The code comment says populated industries count as live, so the rule is broader than the status name suggests.

sections.name: companyKey
sections.title: Company identifier
sections.what: Returns the company's id, or its name if there is no id.
sections.why: Gives a stable key for companies when lists are built.
sections.watch_out: Companies with no id but the same name will be treated as one company.

sections.name: applyFilters
sections.title: Narrowing the project list by filters
sections.what: Takes the full portfolio and returns only the projects that match the chosen industry, country, phase, company, segment and search text. The filtered list feeds the portfolio views.
sections.why: Likely reason: all filter rules sit in one place so every view shows the same projects. The skip argument lets a filter's own dropdown still list all of its options while the other filters apply.
sections.watch_out: The search text is matched only against the project name, country, segment and company names, so a new searchable field must be added here.

sections.name: fmtCapex
sections.title: Showing money in millions or billions
sections.what: Turns a budget in millions of dollars into short text such as $850M or $4.2B. Shows n/a when there is no usable number.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps money figures short and consistent across the app.
sections.watch_out: Values just under 1000 can round up, so 999.9 shows as $1,000M instead of $1B.

sections.name: fmtCapexCoverage
sections.title: Total with count of reported values
sections.what: Shows a total budget and, when only some projects report a value, adds how many did, such as 3/5 reported. Shows Not reported when there is no total.
sections.why: Likely reason: readers need to know that a total may leave out projects with no figure.
sections.watch_out: When the known count is zero the text says Not reported even if a total value was passed in.

sections.name: fmtInt
sections.title: Formatting whole numbers with separators
sections.what: Shows a count such as 1,234 using the number format of the visitor's browser.
sections.why: Likely reason: makes large counts easier to read.
sections.watch_out: The separator style depends on each visitor's browser language, so two users may see different formats.

sections.name: phaseLabel
sections.title: Turning phase codes into readable labels
sections.what: Changes a stored phase code such as UNDER_CONSTRUCTION into a label such as Under Construction.
sections.why: Likely reason: stored codes are built for machines, while people need plain words.
sections.watch_out: It converts any text it receives, so a new phase code appears automatically without any check that it is valid.

sections.name: PHASE_COLOR_FIXED, PHASE_FALLBACK
sections.title: Fixed colors for known project phases
sections.what: Gives set colors to the well-known phases, such as operating, construction, planned and cancelled. Any other phase gets a color from a fallback list that repeats.
sections.why: Likely reason: the main phases keep the same color on every chart.
sections.watch_out: The fallback list has only seven colors, so when there are many unknown phases some colors will repeat.

sections.name: phaseColor
sections.title: Choosing a color for one phase
sections.what: Returns the fixed color for a known phase. For an unknown phase it picks a fallback color based on its position in the list it is given.
sections.why: Likely reason: so unknown phases still receive distinct colors without a hand-made list.
sections.watch_out: A phase missing from the list gets the first fallback color, and changing the list order changes colors for unknown phases.

sections.name: ParsedDate
sections.title: Shape of a parsed date
sections.what: Describes a date after it is read: the year, the quarter when a month is known (empty when only the year is known), and a time number used for sorting.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets code tell a year-only date apart from a full date.
sections.watch_out: The code marks the time number as approximate, so use it for ordering and rough comparisons rather than exact timing.

sections.name: parseDate, Milestone
sections.title: Reading a date string safely
sections.what: Reads a date written as year and month, year month and day, or a bare year, and returns a structured date. Any other text returns nothing, so the page can show a placeholder. Also defines the three milestone names used for project dates.
sections.why: Likely reason: source data is messy, so impossible or unreadable dates are rejected rather than guessed. The milestone names are defined next to the parser so the two stay together.
sections.watch_out: Forms such as Q1 2024 or March 2024 are not read here, unlike the more flexible parser on the Analysis page.

sections.name: MILESTONES
sections.title: Three project milestones and their labels
sections.what: Lists the three key project dates shown to users: FID (final investment decision), construction start, and completion (COD), with the wording each one uses.
sections.why: Likely reason: one list drives the milestone menus and tables so labels stay the same everywhere.
sections.watch_out: A new milestone needs an entry here and a matching lookup in the next section, or it will show no date.

sections.name: milestoneRaw
sections.title: Picking the raw date for a milestone
sections.what: Returns the stored date text for FID, construction start, or completion. Any other milestone returns the completion date.
sections.why: Likely reason: a simple lookup so other code does not need to know the stored field names.
sections.watch_out: Any milestone that is not FID or construction start falls through to the completion date, so a new milestone silently shows wrong dates.

sections.name: Group
sections.title: Shape of a grouped total
sections.what: Describes one group in a summary: its label, how many projects it holds, the total budget of those that report one, and how many reported.
sections.why: Likely reason: summary tables need a count, a total and a sense of how complete the total is.
sections.watch_out: The total is empty (not zero) when no project in the group reports a budget, so display code must handle empty values.

sections.name: groupBy
sections.title: Grouping projects and totaling budgets
sections.what: Sorts projects into groups by a chosen field, such as country, and gives each group a count and budget total. Groups with the largest totals come first.
sections.why: Likely reason: summary charts and tables need totals per category.
sections.watch_out: Projects with no value for the field are placed in a group named Unknown, which can hide missing data in a chart.

sections.name: CompanyAgg
sections.title: Shape of a company summary
sections.what: Describes one company across all its projects: its name, website, whether it is a recorded company, its roles, its projects, its budget total and the industries it appears in.
sections.why: Likely reason: company pages and lists need all of this in one object.
sections.watch_out: The recorded flag is worked out from the start of the company key, so that key format must stay consistent.

sections.name: aggregateCompanies
sections.title: Rolling projects up to companies
sections.what: Goes through every project and every company listed on it, building one summary per company. Companies are sorted by number of projects, then by budget.
sections.why: Likely reason: the companies view needs per-company totals without counting the same project twice for one company.
sections.watch_out: A company listed twice on one project counts once for totals, but all of its roles are kept, and the first website found is the one used.

sections.name: sumCapex, UpcomingBucket
sections.title: Adding up known budgets
sections.what: Adds up the budgets that are present across a list of projects and reports how many had one. The total stays empty when none do. Also defines the timing bucket names used for upcoming dates.
sections.why: Likely reason: missing budgets should not count as zero, and the page must say when a total covers only some projects.
sections.watch_out: Always show the known count next to the total, because the total can look complete when it is not.

sections.name: UPCOMING_LABELS
sections.title: Plain labels for timing buckets
sections.what: Gives the wording shown for each timing group, such as Next 12 months, 3 to 5 years, or No usable date.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the wording in one place.
sections.watch_out: Every timing bucket needs a label here, or the page will show a blank heading for it.

sections.name: upcomingBucket, LocKind
sections.title: Sorting a project into a timing bucket
sections.what: Decides when a project's date falls: already passed, next 12 months, 1 to 3 years, 3 to 5 years, beyond 5 years, this year, or no usable date. Year-only dates are compared by calendar year, and full dates by months from now. Also defines the three levels of location precision.
sections.why: Likely reason: upcoming-project views need to show how soon each milestone is.
sections.watch_out: The current date is read at call time, so buckets change as time passes and a project can move to a different group without any data change.

sections.name: locate
sections.title: Finding a map position for a project
sections.what: Returns map coordinates for a project. It uses exact coordinates if the project has them, otherwise a rough central point for its country, and otherwise returns nothing.
sections.why: Likely reason: many projects lack exact coordinates, so the map can still place them roughly.
sections.watch_out: A country center can be far from the real site in large countries, so the precision label must be shown to the reader.

sections.name: toCsv
sections.title: Writing rows as a spreadsheet file
sections.what: Turns rows of values into comma-separated text that spreadsheets can open. Values with commas, quotes or line breaks are wrapped in quotes.
sections.why: Likely reason: supports the export feature so users can work with the data in a spreadsheet.
sections.watch_out: Text starting with an equals, plus, minus, at sign or tab gets an apostrophe in front, which changes the text in the exported file.

sections.name: downloadCsv
sections.title: Triggering the file download in the browser
sections.what: Builds a CSV file from rows and starts a download in the visitor's browser under the given file name.
sections.why: Likely reason: browsers can save a file this way without a server step.
sections.watch_out: The temporary download link is removed after one second, a fixed delay that does not confirm the download has finished.

sections.name: projectCsvRows
sections.title: Columns for the project export
sections.what: Builds the rows for a project export: a header line, then one row per project with its identity, phase, budget, dates, location, capacity and companies with their roles.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed header means every export has the same columns in the same order.
sections.watch_out: Companies are joined with semicolons, so a company name containing a semicolon makes the column harder to split again.

sections.name: websiteHost
sections.title: Extracting a safe website domain
sections.what: Pulls the domain name from a recorded website address, adding https when the scheme is missing. Returns nothing if the address cannot be read.
sections.why: The code comment says the domain is never guessed, so displayed domains come only from recorded data.
sections.watch_out: Only the domain is kept, so a link built from it goes to the site's home page, not the page the address pointed to.

summary: Holds the portfolio data layer: fetching and checking the portfolio response, and the filter, grouping, and export helpers that portfolio screens use.
purpose: Lets portfolio screens load one checked dataset and filter it the same way everywhere.
why: The comment says the validator throws on bad data rather than silently fixing it, so problems are visible.
how: Fetches the portfolio, checks its shape, and caches it for one minute. Reads filter settings from the address. Filters projects by scope, industry, and other settings, and groups companies. Only the first seven sections were supplied, so the rest of the file is not described here.
inputs: The server response at /api/portfolio, and filter values from the address.
outputs: A checked portfolio, filter settings, and helper results used by portfolio pages.
risks: If the server changes its shape, the validator throws and the page fails. The scope rule for industries has a note that may confuse future readers.
debug: If a portfolio page is blank, check the error message from the validator, which names the bad index. Compare the server response with the checks.
